thread.title: University of Washington Primate Research Sparks Debate After PETA Video Release
thread.title_full: University of Washington Primate Research Sparks Debate After PETA Video Release

author: fox13seattle
title: University of Washington Primate Research Sparks Debate After PETA Video Release
text:
PETA video shows infant monkeys in experiments at University of Washington, reigniting debate over primate research. UW says the experiments ended years ago.
Newly released video showing infant monkeys undergoing experiments at a University of Washington research laboratory is reigniting a decades-old debate over whether primates are still necessary for biomedical research. The footage, obtained by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals through a public records request, shows infant macaques, some only days old, lying on laboratory tables with their heads shaved and electrodes attached to their bodies as researchers test their development.
The experiments shown in the video took place about six years ago, but PETA says similar research involving young monkeys has continued at the University of Washington. The group argues that advances in technology have made the use of primates unnecessary.
University officials say the particular experiments shown in the footage ended years ago. They maintain that animal research has contributed important information about risks to human health that could not always be obtained through other methods.
Debate Over Primate Research Need
Dr. Lisa Jones-Engel, PETA's chief science advisor on primate issues, said the age of the video does not diminish its relevance. She stated that experiments with infant newborn macaques continue to occur at the university.
Jones-Engel spent 17 years at the University of Washington and has worked as a primate scientist for about 35 years. She is now one of the university's most vocal critics on the use of monkeys in research.
She said that newborns are still being taken from their mothers, animals who should be with their mothers, holding onto them and nursing, yet they are seen on a lab table. PETA obtained the footage through a public records request, a process that took about seven months.
Jones-Engel said PETA released the video because the organization believes the public should see what happens to animals used in research instead of viewing the issue only through scientific papers or descriptions of experiments. She said the group wants people to see these monkeys for who they are and to understand what this experimentation means to these animals.
Substances Studied and Health Implications
University of Washington officials do not dispute that the footage is disturbing. Dr. Sally Thompson-Iritani, the university's assistant vice provost for animal care, said she has watched the video several times and understands the reaction people are feeling. She said it is hard to watch and does not want to minimize that in any fashion.
But she said the images alone do not explain why the experiments were performed or what researchers were trying to learn. The research examined what could happen to developing offspring when pregnant animals were exposed to substances including methylmercury and domoic acid.
Domoic acid is a naturally occurring marine toxin that can accumulate in seafood, while methylmercury can also enter the human food supply, particularly through some types of fish. Researchers were attempting to determine how exposure during pregnancy might affect neurological development and whether harm could appear later rather than immediately after birth.
Thompson-Iritani said that some effects with low-level exposure to these contaminants might not be seen even at birth. They sometimes show up later in development.
The university says research involving primates can help scientists understand how exposure during pregnancy could affect human development and potentially help determine what exposure levels are dangerous.
Dispute Over Post-Research Fate
Another point of dispute involves what happens to animals after research is completed. Jones-Engel said that we do not need to rely upon an infant monkey taken from their mother and experimented on to tell us how drugs and treatments can improve human health.
Asked whether it was accurate that animals would have to be killed after an experiment and why, Thompson-Iritani said scientists sometimes need to examine organs or other tissue to fully evaluate the biological effects being studied. The debate continues over whether monkeys should still be used in biomedical research.
